newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - BULL RUN DECLARED DONE.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - BULL RUN DECLARED DONE.

text.p: It had to end sooner or later, but U.S. government securities traders didn't expect the market's bull run to come to quite such an abrupt halt.
But, with prices down more than four points and yields up as much as 40 basis points in a week, that's what analysts said has occurred.

"We go back to establishing a trading range," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co. "We were trading at ludicrious levels and Friday provided a wake-up call to the end of the bull market run."
Late Friday, the 30-year cash bond was at 96-19/32, down 1-1/2 points. Its yield soared to 6.64 percent from 6.52 percent from Thursday, its highest level since closing at 6.72 percent on July 2.
That followed a sharp sell-off on Thursday.

"This has been one of the worst two back-to-back days I have ever seen," said Dave Connors, head trader at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. But players said the market was not out of the woods yet as it has to contend with Wednesday's retail sales report for July.
The consensus is for a 0.5 to 0.6 percent rise in retail sales. But the market fears for a stronger number.

For one, William Sullivan, director of money markets reserach at Dean Witter Securities, said he has bumped up his forecast to a 0.9 to 1.0 rise due to very strong auto and chain store sales figures in July.
Therefore, the market is seen remaining under pressure.
"The market is still vulnerable," Connors said. "There is no reason this (selloff) doesn't continue. We could see 6.75 on the bond."
Analysts now see the 30-year bond in a 6.50 percent range, and two-year notes -- as low as 5.74 percent last week -- in a 6.00 to 6.25 range, levels that are seen as "fair value."

"We have got to find buyers for this paper," Strauss said, referring to the $38 billion in three- and 10-year notes the Treasury sold this week that retail refused to buy. "The risk is that we cheapen up a little more."
He noted that it's not uncommon for the market to correct four or five points after an 11 to 12 point rally, even though he said it usually takes longer than a few trading sessions.

Fundamentally, little has changed, players said. It was just the realization that the economy still has steam left in it, particularly the labor market and consumer spending and the Federal Reserve is still very much in the picture.
Until Wednesday's retail sales data, the market is expected to consolidate.
The only items of interest scheduled are the weekly chain store sales reports, the July Atlanta Fed and Richmond Fed indexes and second quarter productivity/unit labor costs data on Tuesday.
Players said they will also keep an eye on the dollar, since its declines on Friday added to the market's woes.
